## Course Overview & Learning Outcomes

### Course Description
Regression is one of the most widely used statistical techniques across the sciences, social sciences, and industry. This course develops both its theory and its practice: how regression models are built and justified, and how to analyse data when they apply.

We begin with simple linear regression (least squares estimation, the geometry behind it, and inference on the regression parameters under normally distributed errors) then extend to multiple regression in matrix form, covering analysis of variance, confidence and prediction intervals, multicollinearity, and models with both quantitative and qualitative predictors. The last part of the course asks what to do when the standard assumptions fail: diagnostics, model selection and validation, and remedial measures including weighted least squares. All computation is in R, and you will be expected to write R code, interpret its output, and report your conclusions in writing.

### Learning Outcomes
At the completion of this course, students will be able to:
1. Use R software to conduct regression analysis.
2. Carry out and interpret inference procedures for simple and multiple linear regression.
3. Know the multiple linear regression model in its matrix form, including all common variations on this model (e.g., continuous predictors, categorical predictors, square and interaction terms).
4. Understand what are the purposes of diagnostic methods in simple and multiple regression; be able to carry out several common diagnostic procedures and interpret them.
5. Know several measures of model performance, how to compute and interpret them for a multiple regression model.
6. Write an analysis report with real data.

### Course Metadata
- **Prerequisites**: STAB57H3
- **Corequisites**: None
- **Exclusions**: STA302H; [Students who want to complete both STAC67H3 and MGEB12H3, and receive credit for both courses, must successfully complete MGEB12H3 prior to enrolling in STAC67H3; for students who complete MGEB12H3 after successfully completing STAC67H3, MGEB12H3 will be marked as Extra (EXT)].

## Course Materials & Computing Resources

### Textbooks
- **Required Text (Kutner)**:  
  Kutner, M. H., Nachtsheim, C. J., and Neter, J. (2004), *Applied Linear Regression Models*, 4th edition (older editions are fine).  
  - Data sets and solution manual: [http://www.cnachtsheim-text.csom.umn.edu](http://www.cnachtsheim-text.csom.umn.edu)
- **Sub-text (Sheather)**:  
  Simon J. Sheather (2009), *A Modern Approach to Regression with R* (a lighter, R-centred companion, available online for free through the U of T library).

### Statistical Computing in R
All computation in this course is in **R**, and you are expected to write R code and interpret R output on assignments, quizzes, and tests.

- **R**: Install [The R Project for Statistical Computing](https://www.r-project.org/) (free, all platforms).
- **RStudio**: Install [RStudio Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) as the primary IDE.
- **R Markdown**: Reports are written in [R Markdown](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/lesson-1.html), which produces a PDF or HTML document from code and prose in one file (covered in Tutorial 1).
- **ggplot2 & Tidyverse**: Figures use [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/).
- **Required R Packages**:
  ```r
  install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "car", "leaps", "MASS", "glmnet"))
  ```
- **Cheat Sheets & References**:
  - [R for Data Science (2e)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/)
  - [R Markdown Cheat Sheet](https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/)
  - [ggplot2 Cheat Sheet](https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/)

### Final Grade Formulas

$$\text{Final Grade} = 15\% \, (\text{Assignments}) + 15\% \, (\text{Quizzes}) + 15\% \, (\text{Midterm}) + \max \Big\{ 20\% \, (\text{Project}) + 35\% \, (\text{Final Exam}), \; 55\% \, (\text{Final Exam}) \Big\}$$

- **Dual Calculation**: Your grade is calculated twice: once counting the project, and once with that weight moved onto the final exam. You receive whichever result is higher.
- **Zero Risk**: Both marks are out of 100, so the comparison is simple: the project counts whenever your project mark is higher than your final exam mark, and is ignored otherwise. Doing the project can raise your grade and can never lower it. If you do not do the project, your final exam is worth **55%**.
- **Leaving the Project**: The project has four deadlines:
  1. Group and dataset declared (**Friday, Nov 6**)
  2. Checkpoint (**Friday, Nov 13**)
  3. Written report (**Friday, Nov 27**)
  4. Presentation (**Week of Nov 30 / Dec 4**)
  If you miss any of them, you are simply assessed on the second formula for the rest of the term, with the final exam worth 55%. This is not an academic penalty and you do not receive a zero; you are treated exactly as a student who chose not to do the project. Leaving is an individual decision: the rest of your group may carry on, and your report mark is discarded only for you.
- **Midterm Policy**: The midterm test is not optional and is not part of this calculation. If you miss it for a documented valid reason, its weight is transferred to your final exam.

### Quizzes
- **Format**: Three quizzes written during designated tutorial sessions.

- **Coverage**: Each quiz covers material up to the Friday of the preceding week:
  - **Quiz 1**: Week 4 tutorial (covers through Friday Sep 25 / Oct 2)
  - **Quiz 2**: Week 8/9 tutorial (covers through Friday Oct 23)
  - **Quiz 3**: Week 11/12 tutorial (covers through Friday Nov 20)
- **Make-up Policy**: **There are NO make-up quizzes for any reason.** The dropped quiz accommodation accounts for illness or emergencies.

### Optional Case Study Project

- **Components**:

## Course Policies & University Statements

### Academic Integrity
The University treats cases of cheating and plagiarism very seriously. The University of Toronto's [Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters](http://www.governingcouncil.utoronto.ca/policies/behaveac.htm) outlines behaviours constituting academic dishonesty:
- **Papers & Assignments**: Using someone else's ideas or words without appropriate acknowledgement, submitting work in more than one course without instructor permission, falsifying sources or data, or obtaining unauthorized assistance.
- **Tests & Exams**: Using or possessing unauthorized aids, looking at someone else's answers, misrepresenting identity, or altering documentation.

### Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Policy
- **Permitted Uses**: Students may use artificial intelligence tools, including generative AI, in this course as learning aids or to help produce assignments. However, **students are ultimately accountable for the work they submit**.
- **Prohibited Uses**: Students **may NOT use artificial intelligence tools for taking tests or examinations**.
- **Academic Offense**: The knowing use of generative AI tools (ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, etc.) for the completion of, or to support the completion of, an examination, term test, or unauthorized assessment constitutes an academic offense.

### Missed Assessments & Late Policies
- **Late Submissions**: Late submission of any assessment will NOT be allowed.
- **Quizzes**: Lowest of three dropped automatically. No make-ups.
- **Midterm**: If missed for a documented valid reason, its weight is transferred to the final exam.
- **Project Deadlines**: To be counted, groups must declare members and claim a dataset by Nov 6 and pass the checkpoint on Nov 13. Late reports are not accepted.
